Modeled utility bill impact and emissions reduction potential Using the electricity rates from the electric utility in PBC, Florida Power and Light (FPL), and the data presented in Figure 11, it is possible to estimate the annual utility bill impact for each upgrade package. According to the FPL’s Residential Service Electricity Rate, residents who use less than 1,000 kWh of electricity a month are charged $0.22637/kWh.11 Based on Figure 14, we can ascertain that upgrading low-income households in PBC to an ENERGY STAR (Upgrade 1) or Ultra-high Efficiency (Upgrade 3) Heat Pump would decrease median annual utility bills of most of these households by ~$150 to ~$490, respectively. In a similar analysis to that done for Figure 11, we can infer that full electrification using high-efficiency appliances (Upgrades 11 and 13) can save households ~$200 each year on their utility bills. Finally, as discussed previously, the addition of the Light Touch Envelope upgrade package does little to lower utility bills for low-income PBC residents. Another analysis that can be done using the ResStock data for PBC is the emissions (kg-CO e) 2 reduction potential for these upgrades. Using the Mid-Case 15-year Long-run Marginal Emission Rates for electricity from the Cambium dataset, it is possible to calculate the median change in annual household emissions for each upgrade12 (Figure 15). The modeled reduction potential of these upgrades is generally proportional to the utility bill savings, with the upgrades that include the Ultra-high Efficiency Heat Pump measure (Upgrades 3, 8, and 13) creating the largest emissions reduction potential. Summary Limitations This analysis was based in large part on publicly available data produced by the ResStock model. It is important to note that this model has the following limitations: • Analysis is based on ResStock modeled energy consumption, and all models have uncertainties. For example, discrepancies in assumptions of HVAC setpoints and occupant behaviors could introduce gaps between modeled and realized energy savings for a home upgrade project. • ResStock models do not account for energy-conserving behaviors (e.g., not using an appliance due to bill concerns), broken equipment, or other housing conditions requiring remediation (e.g., mold and moisture, broken windows), which may be prevalent in some housing. • Upgrade costs do not account for additional services that may be needed to perform home upgrades—namely, electrical service upgrades. • Description of the building stock is based on national surveys and datasets, which may hide local unique characteristics
